newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraqi minister discusses speeding up food purchases.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi minister discusses speeding up food purchases.

text.p: Iraqi Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf discussed with the president of the Security Council on Wednesday how to accelerate procedures under an "oil-for-food" deal that took effect last December.

"Any practical person will see that up to now not one gram of food or medicine has reached Iraq," he said, referring to humanitarian supplies that Baghdad is buying with a portion of the $2 billion worth of oil it is allowed to sell over a six-month period.
Al-Sahaf said he had offered council President Njunguna Mahugu of Kenya "some suggestions how to accelerate those procedures" regarding the approval of contracts by the council's sanctions committee.

Speaking to reporters after a 30-minute meeting, he said he had also briefed Mahugu on "positive steps" that had resulted from recent meetings in Baghdad between Iraqi officials and ambassador Rolf Ekeus, the head of the U.N. special commission in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction.

"Now it is much, much clearer than before that the so-called pattern of concealment...is baseless. Such concerns do not stand on solid ground," he said, referring to repeated assertions by UNSCOM and others that Iraq had systematically attempted to hide some of the weapons it was required to surrender for destruction under Gulf War resolutions.
"Now it is clearer in the minds of the special commission that there is no concealment behaviour from the Iraqi side, and this is very important," al-Sahaf added.

Ekeus said in Baghdad last Sunday that Iraq had agreed to allow the removal for study abroad of remnants of more than 100 missile engines that Iraq said it had destroyed in 1992 without U.N. supervision. Iraq had for several months balked at the export of the engines, which were buried but unearthed last year.

UNSCOM wants to establish whether they are from Soviet-made engines, as Iraq maintains, or were locally manufactured. This is part of the commission's effort to establish whether all Iraq's nuclear, biological, chemical and missile inventories have been fully accounted for.

Ekeus also said UNSCOM still had "quite substantial and serious" concerns about Iraq's chemical arms and that the two sides agreed to put off discussion of Iraq's banned biological warfare programme until his next visit.
